claims.claim: In a UK interview study, 22 people aged 71 to 98 with Clinical Frailty Scale 5 to 8 (mild to very severe frailty), a quarter of them living with dementia, were interviewed in their first 72 hours in hospital about what they wanted from acute care.
claims.supporting_passage: "Participants aged over 65 with Clinical Frailty Score 5-8 (mild to very severe frailty) were recruited during their first 72 hours in a UK hospital." ... "The 22 participants were aged 71 to 98 and had mild to very severe frailty. One quarter were living with dementia. Most participants had reflected on their situation and considered their outcome goals."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty (CFS 5 to 8) in emergency or acute hospital care, one UK hospital; semi-structured interviews within the first 72 hours; outcome goals for acute care; no comparator.
claims.safe_wording: Researchers interviewed 22 people aged 71 to 98 living with frailty, a quarter of them with dementia, in their first three days in a UK hospital, and asked what they wanted from their care.
claims.qualifications: One hospital, 22 people, qualitative. Say 'a small interview study' and give the number. The paper calls the scale the 'Clinical Frailty Score'; the scale's usual name is Clinical Frailty Scale.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that contradicts the themes; Phelps 2022 (C05-13-j) reports similar goals in a different sample.

numbers.meaning: age range of participants in years
inclusion range, described as mild to very severe frailty
timing of recruitment after arrival in hospital
proportion of the 22 living with dementia

claims.claim: The outcome goals grouped into 'Autonomy' (information, control, security) and 'Functioning' (physical, psychosocial, relief); 'relief' meant relief from distressing symptoms.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Theme categories (and corresponding sub-categories) were 'Autonomy' (information, control, and security) and 'Functioning' (physical, psychosocial, and relief)." Full text: "In choosing to attend for acute healthcare, participants sought relief from distressing symptoms and support to overcome limitations in physical and psychosocial function."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Results (full-text excerpt via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: What they wanted fell into two groups. One was having some control: understanding what was happening, having a say, and feeling safe. The other was being able to function: to move and do things, to keep up their relationships and activities, and to get relief from distressing symptoms.
claims.qualifications: These are themes, not frequencies; do not say 'most people wanted X' except for security (see C05-13-c). For the visual, 'to have a say' should be qualified by C05-13-e (to be asked how much say they want).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors note the boundaries between categories were indistinct.

claims.claim: A theme new to the literature was security: participants wanted to feel safe in their usual living place and with their health problems; this was common to most participants.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A novel 'security' theme was identified, whereby participants sought to feel safe in their usual living place and with their health problems." Full text (Conclusions): "The novel sub-theme 'security', comprising feeling safe in living place, routine, and health, was common to most interview participants."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Conclusions (full-text excerpt via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: A goal the researchers had not seen described before was security: wanting to feel safe at home, in their routine and with their health problems. Most of the 22 people raised it.
claims.qualifications: 'Novel' is the authors' description relative to earlier studies of older people in general.

numbers.meaning: participants for whom the security theme was common (not quantified further)

claims.claim: People with milder frailty were concerned to keep supporting loved ones; those with the most severe frailty were concerned about being a burden on others.
claims.supporting_passage: "Those living with milder frailty were concerned to maintain ability to support loved ones, while those living with most severe frailty were concerned about burdening others."
claims.location: Abstract, Results (complete in the PubMed record)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C05-13-a; comparison across frailty severity within the 22 participants.
claims.safe_wording: People with milder frailty wanted to keep being able to help the people they love. People with the most severe frailty worried about being a burden on others.
claims.qualifications: Pattern within a small qualitative sample; not a measured difference. The word 'burden' here is the participants' concern, which STYLE.md allows; do not describe older people as a burden.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. The candidate's note that the severe-frailty finding was cut off is resolved: the full abstract is in PubMed.

claims.claim: Not all participants wanted to be active decision-makers; participants with frailty wished first to be asked how involved they wanted to be.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text (Results): "Participants preferred varying degrees of active involvement in healthcare decision-making personally or with relatives and wished to be consulted on this." Full text (Discussion): "Older people in general wished to be active decision-makers, whereas that was not always the case among these participants with frailty, who first wished to be asked about their preferred degree of involvement."
claims.location: Results and Discussion (full-text excerpts via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: Not everyone wanted to make the decisions themselves. Some wanted relatives involved. What they wanted was to be asked how involved they wished to be.
claims.qualifications: Supports a closing question for staff, such as 'How much do you want to be involved in decisions about your care today, and who else should be part of them?' Present the question as a suggestion drawn from the study, not as a tested intervention.

claims.claim: Acute care for older people is usually judged by service measures such as waiting times and time targets, length of stay, readmission and deaths, which the researchers argue may not capture what older people living with frailty consider meaningful.
claims.supporting_passage: van Oppen 2022, Introduction (Scite citation-context excerpt): "As emergency departments (ED) worldwide become crowded increasingly frequently, poorer attainment of time targets can be expected" ... "Older people living with frailty are at particular risk of prolonged length of stay, as well as other adverse outcomes including mortality and functional decline. These outcomes are service metrics and, while useful for managers, may not capture what older people consider meaningful." van Oppen 2024, Abstract (Background): "Current acute healthcare service metrics are not meaningful for older people living with frailty. Healthcare knowledge, situational security, and physical and psychosocial function are important outcomes typically not collected." Phelps 2022, Discussion (Scite citation-context excerpt): "Emergency care research and quality improvement usually focuses upon service metrics such as length of stay and readmission rates, which do not necessarily align with patient perspectives."
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' description of current emergency and acute care quality measures; not a survey or audit of what services record.
claims.safe_wording: Emergency care is usually judged on things like waiting times, length of stay and readmissions. The research team behind this study argue that these measures miss much of what people living with frailty want from their care, such as understanding what is happening and feeling safe.
claims.qualifications: These are the authors' statements in introductions and discussions, not measured findings. Do not say services 'never' or 'do not' record these outcomes as a fact; say they are 'usually judged on' service measures and attribute the argument. The visual's left column ('time in the department, admitted or not, length of stay') is fair as a description of common service measures.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some services do use patient-reported experience measures; no audit of UK acute care measures was opened in this batch.

claims.claim: A systematic review found no patient-reported outcome measure designed for older people with frailty in emergency care; the existing measures mainly assessed functioning, with limited coverage of autonomy.
claims.supporting_passage: "There is no person-reported outcome measure (PROM) for older people with frailty and emergency care needs." ... "Of 9392 unique citations screened, we appraised the full texts of 158 studies. Nine studies were identified, evaluating nine PROMs." ... "PROMs mainly assessed 'Functioning' constructs, with limited coverage of 'Autonomy'."
claims.pico_timeframe: PROMs used 2010 to 2021 by older people living with frailty in acute hospital care; mapping of instrument content against the Autonomy and Functioning framework.
claims.safe_wording: When the same team reviewed existing questionnaires in 2022, the ones used with older people in acute care mostly asked about physical and daily functioning. Few asked about understanding, control or feeling safe.
claims.qualifications: Situation up to 2021; PROM-OPAC has since been developed (C05-13-h). Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The mapping uses the authors' own framework.

numbers.meaning: PROMs identified in 9 studies (from 9392 citations screened)

claims.claim: A patient-reported outcome measure built on these goals (PROM-OPAC) was field-tested with 241 people living with frailty within 72 hours of an emergency attendance and had acceptable reliability; further evaluation is needed.
claims.supporting_passage: "People aged 65+ with Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8 were recruited within seventy-two hours of an emergency attendance." ... "241 people participated." ... "The final eight-item draft had acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha: 0.71), structure (two factors for self-determination and security; RMSEA: 0.065; TLI: 0.917; CFI: 0.944), and construct validity (lower scores from respondents waiting longer and requiring admission). Feasibility was promising (response rate 39%; 98% responses complete; median completion time 11 (IQR: 12) minutes)." ... "Administration of the PROM-OPAC appeared feasible and the instrument had acceptable psychometric properties. Further evaluation is required to assess generalisability."
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 65 and over, CFS 5 to 8, within 72 hours of emergency attendance; three-stage field-testing; cross-sectional.
claims.safe_wording: The team has since built an eight-question measure from these goals, covering self-determination and security. In testing with 241 people living with frailty in emergency care, it worked acceptably, and the authors say it needs further evaluation.
claims.qualifications: Say 'eight-question' and '241 people'. Do not quote Cronbach's alpha or fit indices for the public. The link between lower scores and longer waits or admission is a cross-sectional validity check, not evidence that waiting causes lower scores; if mentioned, say 'people who waited longer or were admitted tended to score lower'. The response rate was 39%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Development by the same group; generalisability not yet shown.

numbers.meaning: participants across the three field-testing stages
items in the final draft measure
Cronbach's alpha (internal consistency); practitioner use only

claims.claim: In a 2026 study, 60 older people living with frailty and significant cognitive impairment completed PROM-OPAC during emergency care; 92% of responses were complete, with a median time of 8 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: "PROM-OPAC is currently the only PROM for Older People living with frailty receiving Acute Care. However, there is limited evidence for its feasibility among the 40% of that cohort who have cognitive impairment." ... "60 people (63% (95% CI 53% to 73%) of 95 approached) with significant cognitive impairment participated (median 6CIT 21/28; IQR 16-25). 92% responses were complete, with median time 8 (IQR 5-11) min. Internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha, 0.70) but the observed response distribution (SD <1 in two items) and end effects suggested interpretability issues." ... "Older people living with frailty and cognitive impairment can complete PROMs during emergency care."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty and significant cognitive impairment, one UK emergency setting; feasibility and reliability; cross-sectional.
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 study found that people living with frailty and significant memory and thinking problems could answer these questions in the emergency department: 60 of 95 people approached took part, and most completed it in about 8 minutes.
claims.qualifications: Single site; some items had interpretability issues. The '40% of that cohort' figure is background from the introduction, not a finding of this study; do not present it as one. Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Interpretability issues noted by the authors.

numbers.meaning: people with significant cognitive impairment approached who took part

claims.claim: A second interview study (24 patients and 16 carers, three English hospitals) found similar goals (diagnosis and resolution of the problem, information for them and relatives, a well-planned discharge home, keeping mobility and function) and participants felt many goals were not attained.
claims.supporting_passage: "Forty participants were interviewed either alone or jointly (24 patients and 16 carers), describing episodes of urgent care which started in ED for 28 patients. The goals of care for participants accessing emergency care were that their medical problem be diagnosed and resolved; information about tests and treatment be given to them and their relatives; they receive an appropriate well-planned discharge to their own home with support where needed and without readmission or re-attendance at ED; and that they retain mobility, function and normal activities. Participants perceived that many of these goals of care were not attained." ... "Older people living with frailty have heterogeneous urgent care goals which require individual ascertainment."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty and carers, three hospitals in England, interviewed after an urgent care episode in 2019.
claims.safe_wording: A separate study of 24 patients and 16 carers in three English hospitals heard similar aims: find and treat the problem, explain it to us and our family, plan a safe discharge home, and help me keep moving. Many felt these aims were not met.
claims.qualifications: 'Not attained' is participants' perception, not a measured rate. Optional corroborating claim; it shows the goals are not unique to one hospital.

numbers.meaning: patients whose care episode started in the emergency department

claims.claim: A 2024 systematic review of 19 studies of older people's experiences of frailty found resistance to the medical use of the term frail.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty-four studies were subsequently excluded as they did not address the systematic review question, leaving 17 included in the final review. An additional two studies were identified via grey literature sources. Older persons' experiences of frailty were synthesised with reference to three themes: (i) living with frailty: a multidimensional experience; (ii) living with frailty: acceptability and associations; and (iii) living with frailty: resisting and adapting and losing control." ... "Older persons' experiences of frailty revealed a resistance to the biomedical use of the term generally used in clinical practice."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older persons living with frailty; qualitative meta-synthesis; literature to January 2024.
claims.safe_wording: A 2024 review brought together 19 studies of older people's own accounts of frailty. Many resisted the medical label 'frail' being applied to them, and described frailty in broader terms than clinicians usually do.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative synthesis; 'many' rather than a proportion. Abstract only. Use this review, not a single study, for the general statement that many older people dislike or resist the word.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schoenborn 2018 (C05-10-d) found people who were frail were more open to discussing frailty than those who were not, so resistance to the word is not the same as not wanting the information.

numbers.meaning: studies included (17 from databases plus 2 from grey literature)

claims.claim: In a 2024 interview study within a home rehabilitation trial, older people saw the frail label as negative and something to avoid, and the authors concluded the term needs to be used cautiously; some participants saw frailty as temporary and reducible with exercise and activity.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ninety three HERO trial participants were sampled for the process evaluation with a total of 60 observational home visits and 35 interviews were undertaken. There was a wide range in perceptions about what it meant to be classified as frail with no clear understanding from our participants. However, there was a negative attitude towards frailty with it being considered something that needed to be avoided where possible. Frailty was seen as part of a negative decline that people struggled to associate with. There was discussion about frailty being temporary and that it could be reduced or avoided with sufficient physical exercise and activity." ... "Having a label of being "frail" was deemed to be negative and something to be avoided, suggesting the term needs to be used cautiously."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people taking part in a home-based rehabilitation trial (HERO); secondary qualitative analysis of interviews and observed visits.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2024 study of 35 interviews with older people in a home rehabilitation trial, being labelled frail was seen as negative and something to avoid. The researchers concluded the word needs to be used with care. Some participants saw frailty as something exercise and activity could reduce.
claims.qualifications: Do not name the country in the post unless checked (author affiliations are UK; abstract does not say). Participants were in a rehabilitation trial.

numbers.meaning: trial participants sampled for the process evaluation

claims.claim: In US focus groups with 29 community-dwelling older adults, participants wanted to know how to treat or prevent frailty and the risks it carries, and many felt this information could be given without the word 'frail', which they saw as negative.
claims.supporting_passage: "The participants' mean age was 76.3. Of the 29 participants, 21 (72%) were female, and 21 (72%) were white." ... "3) Participants wanted know about how to treat or prevent frailty and the risks associated with being frail. Many participants felt that these information can be conveyed without necessarily using the specific term "frail", which they perceived to have a negative connotation." ... Conclusions: "Further research is needed to understand acceptable ways for communicating about frailty in clinical practice." Full text (Discussion): "Furthermore, given the negative reactions to the term "frailty" and that the interventions are not exclusive to frailty, it is conceivable that clinicians may make the appropriate recommendations without having to explicitly discuss frailty."
claims.location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions; Discussion (Scite excerpt)
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older adults in the USA, focus groups stratified by frailty status (Fried criteria); perceptions and informational needs; no comparator intervention.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study, 29 older people in focus groups said they wanted to know their risks and how to prevent or treat frailty. Many felt this could be explained without the word 'frail', which they heard as negative.
claims.qualifications: One small US study; name the size (29 people). The authors call for research on acceptable ways to communicate about frailty: no study has tested which wording works better, so present the 'translate the assessment' approach as a suggestion, not a proven method.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C05-10-d: people who were frail were more willing to hear the word.

claims.claim: In the same study, participants who were frail were more receptive to discussing their frailty status with clinicians than those who were non-frail or pre-frail.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "2) Compared to participants who were non-frail or pre-frail, participants who were frail were more receptive to discussing their frailty status with clinicians". Full text (Results): "On the contrary, both of the focus groups consisting of frail participants were much more amenable to discussing frailty status with clinicians than the non-frail and the pre-frail participants. “We want to know what’s going on and how to treat it and we are not afraid to hear these words, we get more upset that you didn’t tell us.”" Full text (Discussion): "We were surprised to find that the more frail participants were more receptive to discussing frailty, as compared to the non-frail and pre-frail participants." Limitation: "Lastly, for most of the frail participants, several years have lapsed since their frailty assessment and their frailty status may have changed."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Results and Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C05-10-c; comparison between focus groups by frailty status (two frail groups).
claims.safe_wording: In that study, the people who were frail were more willing to talk about frailty with their doctors than those who were not. One participant said: "We want to know what's going on and how to treat it and we are not afraid to hear these words, we get more upset that you didn't tell us."
claims.qualifications: Two focus groups of frail participants in one US study; frailty status had been assessed years earlier for most. The quotation is a participant's words from the published paper and may be quoted with attribution ('a participant in a US study'); do not present it as said to Alasdair or as a UK patient. This finding means the post must not suggest avoiding frank discussion of risk.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Other studies (C05-10-a, C05-10-b, C05-10-e) report resistance to the label among people classed as frail; the difference may reflect willingness to discuss information versus acceptance of the label as an identity.

claims.claim: In an interview study of 29 people aged 66 to 98 in the South West of England, participants described being labelled 'old and frail' by others as encouraging a frailty identity, including loss of interest in social and physical activities; most resisted identifying as frail.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Twenty-nine participants aged 66–98 with varying degrees of frailty, residing either in their homes or institutional settings, participated in semi-structured interviews." ... "Being labelled by others as 'old and frail' contributed to the development of a frailty identity by encouraging attitudinal and behavioural confirmation of it, including a loss of interest in participating in social and physical activities, poor physical health and increased stigmatisation." Full text (Methods): "All participants lived in the South West of England and the sample included both community dwellers and care home residents." Full text (Results): "Most participants actively resisted the identity, even those who could be classified as frail using objective criteria." Full text (Discussion): "As participants in this study expressed, being labelled as frail – particularly against one’s will – was seen as damaging to health, because it may lead to behavioural confirmation of the label." and "The current participants described the readiness of others to label them as frail, often on the basis of isolated events or temporary impairments."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods, Results and Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with varying frailty in the South West of England (home and care home); grounded theory interviews; perceptions only, no measured outcome.
claims.safe_wording: In an English study of 29 people aged 66 to 98, participants described how being called 'old and frail' by others could lead people to see themselves that way and give up activities. Most resisted the label, including some who met frailty criteria.
claims.qualifications: This is what participants described and how the researchers interpreted it; the study did not measure whether labelling reduces activity. Do not write that the word 'causes' people to stop exercising. Say 'may' and attribute it: 'older people in one study described...'. If a direct quotation is used in a post, quote the abstract sentence, since the full-text sentence contains dashes that the house style does not allow.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schoenborn 2018 (C05-10-d) found frail participants more willing to discuss frailty. The authors of this study also note that identifying as frail can sometimes help people get support.

claims.claim: International frailty guidelines recommend, as first-line treatment, a physical activity programme with a resistance (strength) training component, with protein or calorie supplements when weight loss or undernutrition is present, and a fuller assessment for people who screen positive.
claims.supporting_passage: "For individuals screened as positive for frailty, a more comprehensive clinical assessment should be performed to identify signs and underlying mechanisms of frailty (strong recommendation)." ... "First-line therapy for the management of frailty should include a multi-component physical activity programme with a resistance-based training component (strong recommendation). Protein/caloric supplementation is recommended when weight loss or undernutrition are present (conditional recommendation)."
claims.location: Abstract, Recommendations for Screening and Assessment; Recommendations for Management
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with physical frailty; ICFSR guideline 2019, GRADE.
claims.safe_wording: International frailty guidelines recommend an exercise programme that includes strength training as the first step, with extra protein or calories for people who are losing weight or undernourished.
claims.qualifications: The visual's 'strength exercise with enough protein' should become 'exercise that builds strength; extra protein or calories if you are losing weight'. Protein supplements are a conditional recommendation for people losing weight or undernourished, not for everyone.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recommendation for vitamin D, hormones or cognitive therapy; drug treatment not recommended.

claims.claim: Strength training with protein supplementation has the most consistent evidence for delaying or reversing frailty (candidate's wording).
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 925 studies satisfied search criteria and 46 were included. There were 15 690 participants (median study size was 160 participants). Studies reflected a broad heterogeneity." ... "Interventions with both muscle strength training and protein supplementation were consistently placed highest for effectiveness and ease of implementation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Primary care frailty interventions, RCTs and controlled cohorts to May 2017; relative ranking map, no pooled effect.
claims.safe_wording: Use the guideline wording in C05-10-f instead. If this review is cited, say: 'A review of 46 studies in general practice ranked strength training combined with protein supplements highest among the approaches studied.'
claims.qualifications: 'Most consistent evidence' overstates a relative ranking of heterogeneous studies with no pooled effect. Not essential to this post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneous evidence; only a minority of studies measured change in frailty status (see C05-B1, claim C05-07-e).

claims.claim: In a UK study of 73 older migrants from six racialised minority groups, many had not heard the term frailty and did not know what it meant.
claims.supporting_passage: "Photovoice and biographical interviews were used to explore the experience of getting older among 73 participants of 6 different racialised groups living in a UK city." ... "Many of the participants hadn't heard the term frailty and had no understanding of what it might mean." ... "The first theme was more likely to be the case for participants who spoke little English and for those who hadn't been living in the UK for long." ... "Healthcare professionals must consider that older, racially minoritised patients may have never encountered the term frailty before in any type of setting."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older racialised minority migrants in one UK city; qualitative.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2026 UK study of 73 older migrants from six ethnic minority groups, many had never heard the word frailty, especially those who spoke little English or had arrived recently.
claims.qualifications: Optional supporting point for 'ask what the word means to the person'. Qualitative; 'many' is not quantified.

candidates.reason: Reserve candidate. All essential claims are supported by the van Oppen 2022 interview study (PubMed abstract, complete including the severe-frailty sentence, plus full-text excerpts) and the 2024 PROM-OPAC validation. Wording rules: call it a small interview study of 22 people in one UK hospital; present 'acute care is usually judged by waiting times, length of stay and readmissions' as the researchers' argument (C05-13-f), not a measured fact, and do not say services 'do not record' these outcomes. On the visual, replace 'to have a say' with 'to be asked how involved they want to be' (C05-13-e), and describe relief as relief from distressing symptoms (C05-13-b). For the closing question the judge asked for, C05-13-e supports asking 'How much do you want to be involved in decisions today, and who else should be part of them?' presented as a suggestion drawn from the study. The 2026 cognitive-impairment study (C05-13-i) and Phelps 2022 (C05-13-j) are optional and strengthen the point beyond one hospital. No correction or retraction found for any source.

Reserve candidate. The evidence supports the idea, but the draft leans on one small US study and one overstated claim. The general statement that many older people resist the word 'frail' should rest on the 2024 systematic review of 19 studies (C05-10-a), backed by Hall 2024 (C05-10-b). The specific findings (wanting to know risks and what helps; frail participants more open to discussing it) come from one US study of 29 people, which the post must name. Warmoth 2016 is now verified through Scite (not on PubMed): 29 people in the South West of England. It supports only what participants described about labelling and activity, not a measured effect (C05-10-e). The Age UK and BGS 2015 report was not found or opened and must not be cited. 'Strength training with protein has the most consistent evidence' overstates the Travers review; use the ICFSR guideline wording (C05-10-f). No study has tested which way of talking about frailty works better, so the translation approach is a suggestion, and the post should label it as judgement. The judge's values concern holds: the frail participants' quotation ('we get more upset that you didn't tell us') means the post must keep honesty about risk and not advise avoiding the conversation.
candidates.revised_angle: Series: Teaching round (practitioners) or Ask this (public), as the judge suggested. Angle: be honest about risk and careful with the label. A 2024 review of 19 studies found many older people resist the word 'frail' being applied to them. Yet in a US study of 29 people, those who were frail were more willing than others to discuss it, and all wanted to know their risks and what helps; one said 'we get more upset that you didn't tell us'. The practical step, framed as a suggestion: give the assessment as specific findings (for example slower walking, weaker legs), the risk they raise (falls, needing more help), and the actions the guidelines recommend (exercise that builds strength; extra protein or calories if losing weight). Then ask what the word 'frail' means to the person before using it. Optional: some older people have never heard the term (C05-10-h). Visual: keep the comparison card labelled 'Illustrative wording', with the guideline-based action in place of 'enough protein'.
